title: GeoJSON Length Calculator: Lines and Rings
description: Measure great-circle length across GeoJSON lines and polygon rings with the GeoJSON Length Calculator — kilometres and miles. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a sample file’s Times Square–JFK line measures 21.77 km and its square ring adds 3.91 km — 25.68 km of total linework from four features.
quick_answer: The GeoJSON Length Calculator measures the approximate great-circle length of GeoJSON linework — LineStrings, MultiLineStrings and polygon rings — summed segment by segment on the sphere. Paste the file and read the total in kilometres or miles: route lengths, river reaches, boundaries and perimeters from the geometry itself.

Polygon rings measure as perimeters — the fence-line, coastline and constituency numbers that area alone never tells.
A file of road or river segments totals its network length — the denominator for density, cost and maintenance statistics.
A route that was 42.2 km in the planner should be 42.2 km in the exported file. Length is the checksum that catches silent simplification.

popular_table.note: Segments are great-circle arcs on the sphere (Earth radius 6,371 km class) — accurate well within a percent for ordinary lines. Road-following truth needs the road network, not the vertex chain.

faq: Why does my route measure shorter than my GPS track?

Because a stored line cuts corners a walked track does not: GPS logs carry dense points following every bend (plus a little jitter that inflates them), while an exported LineString keeps fewer vertices and straightens the path between them. Same journey, different vertex budgets — the file measures exactly what it holds.
Yes — a hole’s boundary is real linework (an island’s shoreline in a lake district is fenceable geography). If you need outer-only, that is a GIS operation on extracted rings.
The chain through the file’s vertices is measured as it lies. A two-vertex ‘route’ measures the crow’s flight, because that is all the file claims.
Length is horizontal surface length; the third element is ignored. Mountain switchbacks are longer in boots than on this page — honestly so.
Kilometres and miles — 25.68 km is 15.96 miles, and both are printed so nobody converts in their head.
They measure their full walked length, crossings notwithstanding — the chain is summed as drawn.
A segment jumping from 179.9 to −179.9 measures the short way in sane implementations via longitude unwrapping; files that draw the long way across the map have a data smell worth fixing.
